sections.html:
Whatever the grantor owns, a quitclaim hands over, and nothing more. The statute (IC 32-17-2-2) describes the effect as conveying the estate the grantor could convey by a deed of bargain and sale. The grantee therefore stands exactly where the grantor stood.

Indiana also provides a short form in IC 32-21-1-15. A conveyance that says in substance 'A.B. quitclaims to C.D.' works if it describes the property, states the price after the words 'for the sum of,' and carries a signature, a seal and an acknowledgment. The result is a valid quitclaim for the grantee and the grantee's heirs and assigns.

No promise about title appears anywhere in that form. Someone who accepts a quitclaim cannot sue on deed covenants later, and that gap matters most when the buyer is paying money.

sections.h2: What the deed must include to be recorded
sections.html:
A signature alone will not get a deed accepted. The recorder also looks for a notarial act, two mailing addresses, a preparer statement and a redaction affirmation about Social Security numbers. Each comes from a specific code section.

  • Acknowledgment or proof. IC 32-21-2-3 calls for a notarial officer's acknowledgment or a proof, and Indiana allows remote notarization under the cited sections.
  • Addresses. The deed states the mailing address for tax statements and the grantee's mailing address. The grantee's address must be a street or rural route address, and the statement goes at the end of the deed beside the preparer statements.
  • Prepared by. IC 36-2-11-15 wants the preparer's name printed, typed, stamped or signed at the end, for example 'This instrument was prepared by' and the name.
  • Redaction. The preparer affirms under penalties of perjury that reasonable care was taken to redact Social Security numbers, unless a law requires them.
  • Names. Each signer's name is printed under the signature and kept identical throughout, including the notary block.
  • Format. Margins are at least 2 inches top and bottom on the first and last pages, paper is white and no larger than 8.5 by 14 inches, and bound or continuous-form pages are refused.

A deed signed outside Indiana is treated differently on one point: instruments executed or acknowledged outside the state are exempt from the preparer statement rule, and a foreign-language document needs an English translation.

The base county recorder fee for an ordinary deed is $25 under IC 36-2-7-10, and the sales disclosure filing adds $20 when it applies. Counties may add small charges by ordinance, so the recorder's current schedule controls.

Recording itemAmount
Recording a deed (standard pages)$25 flat

Affordable housing fund (some counties)$10 per document

If you are budgeting for a family transfer, ask the county auditor whether the endorsement carries a charge, and expect a notary fee on top.

sections.h2: Auditor endorsement and the sales disclosure form
sections.html:
Two offices handle a deed before it is filed: the county auditor, then the recorder. Many transfers need a sales disclosure form as well. Under IC 36-2-11-14, the recorder can record a land conveyance only after the auditor has endorsed it 'duly entered for taxation subject to final acceptance for transfer,' 'not taxable,' or 'duly entered for taxation.'

The disclosure rules are narrower. A form is required whenever a real property interest moves for valuable consideration in a deed, contract, judgment or similar document. Exempt from the form altogether are quitclaim deeds that do not serve as a source of title, gifts with no valuable consideration, mortgages and transfers to a government unit. Foreclosure, divorce, court-ordered, condemnation and probate transfers need the form but owe no fee.

The transferor and the transferee sign the form, the county assessor reviews and stamps it, and it then goes to the auditor. The auditor may not accept a conveyance when the form is missing, incomplete or unstamped. Each parcel needs its own form, although one form can cover contiguous parcels in the same taxing district under a single deed.

sections.h2: Transfer on death deed versus quitclaim
sections.html:
A transfer on death deed is a different tool. It names who receives the house after the owner dies, and it follows its own rules. IC 32-17-14-11 requires the deed to be on record with the county recorder before death. No consideration, no delivery and no auditor endorsement is needed.

How the owner holds title changes the outcome. On tenancy by the entirety property the deed is void unless the other spouse joins. A joint tenancy with survivorship is severed and becomes a tenancy in common. Once such a deed is recorded, IC 32-21-1-15(b) voids any later conveyance of the property that was not recorded before the owner's death. Owners who may sell later should look at the county records before they act.

sections.h2: Transfer on death deed versus quitclaim
sections.html:
Deeding a house while a tax sale redemption period is running brings in a special rule. IC 32-21-8-7 keeps the auditor from endorsing the conveyance until the buyer has paid the county treasurer the full amount needed to redeem under IC 6-1.1-25 and has shown written proof. Unless the deed is recorded before the redemption period ends, it is void.

A quitclaim does not skip any step here. The treasurer is paid, the auditor endorses and the recorder files, in that order, while the one-year redemption period for ordinary tax sales keeps running.

If you are the grantor and a redemption deadline is close, call the county treasurer first for the payoff figure, because the other two offices cannot act until that payment is shown.

sections.h2: Property in a tax sale redemption period
sections.html:
Deeding a house during a tax sale redemption period triggers a special rule. Under IC 32-21-8-7, the auditor cannot endorse the conveyance until the buyer has paid the county treasurer the full redemption amount under IC 6-1.1-25 and shown written proof. The conveyance is also void unless it is recorded by the end of the redemption period.

A quitclaim in that situation is no shortcut. The treasurer's payoff, the auditor's endorsement and the recorder's filing all have to happen in order, and the one-year redemption period for ordinary tax sales runs on its own clock.

sections.h2: Selling a house after a quitclaim transfer
sections.html:
A cash buyer still needs the chain of title to hold together, so a recent quitclaim among family members raises questions a title company will ask. Who signed, whether all owners joined, whether the deed was recorded and whether a sales disclosure form went in with it are the points that decide how fast a closing moves.

Recent quitclaims also affect property tax benefits. The homestead deduction is tied to the owner's principal residence, and current rules add a 10 percent penalty for keeping a deduction after ineligibility. An owner who stops living in a house after deeding it should notify the county auditor.

Before you list, pull the recorded deed and confirm the names match your ID and the tax bill. A mismatch is easy to fix before an offer and slow to fix after one.

faqs.q: Is a quitclaim deed legal in Indiana?
faqs.a: Yes. IC 32-21-1-15 recognizes a conveyance worded in substance as 'A.B. quitclaims to C.D.' if it describes the property, states the consideration and is signed, sealed and acknowledged.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: The recorder charges $25 for an ordinary deed under IC 36-2-7-10, with a $25 plus $5 per extra page schedule for oversized pages. A sales disclosure form adds a $20 fee paid to the county auditor when the transfer is for value.

faqs.q: Does a quitclaim deed need a notary?
faqs.a: Yes. IC 32-21-2-3 requires an acknowledgment or a proof, and Indiana allows a remote notary under the cited statutes.

faqs.q: Do I need a sales disclosure form for a quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: Not always. Quitclaim deeds that do not serve as a source of title, and gifts with no valuable consideration, are exempt. A transfer for valuable consideration does need one.

faqs.q: Does a quitclaim deed guarantee clear title?
faqs.a: No. It passes only the interest the grantor has under IC 32-17-2-2, and the short statutory form contains no title promises.
